cases.name: doc-english-sufficient
cases.promptMarkdown:
We're a Dutch manufacturer, Class IIa device, selling into Germany among other markets.
Our EU Declaration of Conformity is in English only. Our distributor says everything
has to be translated into German for the German market. Do we need to translate the
Declaration of Conformity?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MPDG § 8(1): the manufacturer must make the EU Declaration of Conformity available "in
deutscher oder in englischer Sprache" — German OR English. English alone is compliant.
The distributor is wrong about the DoC specifically.

PASS requires:
(1) The answer is NO, the Declaration of Conformity does not need translating —
    English alone satisfies § 8(1).
(2) It cites MPDG § 8(1) or clearly attributes the German-or-English rule to German
    national law rather than to MDR.
(3) It distinguishes the DoC from information for users and patients, which under
    § 8(2) does default to German. Saying "the DoC is fine in English, but your user
    information is a different question" is the ideal answer.

FAIL if it says the DoC must be translated into German. FAIL if it agrees with the
distributor wholesale, or answers "everything must be in German" — that is the
over-application this case exists to catch, and it is the more common error.

Not required: naming other markets, or MDR Art. 19 itself.

graders.evidence:
## Does the EU Declaration of Conformity need to be translated into German?

**German market:** confirmed — device is made available in Germany, so MPDG applies
**Answer:** No. For the DoC, German **or** English is sufficient — English alone is compliant. Your distributor is right about the general direction but wrong about the DoC specifically.

| Item | MDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here (MDR Art. 19(1)) `[verify]` | German **or English** — English alone satisfies it | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| Information for users and patients (IFU, labelling) | not carried here | **German**, and it is a *condition of supply* — the product may only be handed over to users/patients if this is met | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, where information is exclusively for professional users | not carried here | English or another easily understood language permitted, but only if **all three**: a justified case (*begründeter Fall*), **exclusively** professional users, and safety-related information still provided in German or the user's language | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 2 `[verified]` |
| Implant information under MDR Art. 18(1), if your IIa device is implantable | not carried here | **German**. No professional-user exception reaches it | MPDG § 8(3) `[verified]` |

The statutory text for the DoC is explicit: *"in deutscher **oder** in englischer Sprache"*. Translating it is over-application, not a compliance improvement — though nothing stops you doing it voluntarily if it smooths the commercial relationship.

So the distributor's "everything must be German" is half right. The DoC is the one item where English is expressly allowed. The user and patient information is where the real obligation sits, and there it is strict — and it is framed as a precondition on supply, not just a documentation duty. If your IFU and labelling are also English-only, that is the thing to fix, not the DoC.

**What would change this:**
- **The professional-user route** — if this IIa device goes exclusively to professional users and you can justify it, § 8(2) sentence 2 opens English for the IFU. But all three conditions are cumulative, and safety-related information still has to be in German (or the user's language) regardless. Miss one condition and the German default snaps back.
- **Implantability** — if your Class IIa device is implantable, the Art. 18(1) implant information is German with no exception available.
- **Field safety notices** — separately, if you ever take a field safety corrective action in Germany, the FSN must be written in German (§ 73(1) `[verified]`), and that attaches to where the action is taken, not where you are established. Worth knowing in advance rather than under time pressure.

One thing I did *not* check, because it sits outside what I can cite: as a Netherlands-established manufacturer you are inside the EU, so the German-establishment duties in § 73(2) sentence 1 (documenting FSCAs and periodically reviewing effectiveness) do not attach to you — but if your German distributor is acting as an importer, they may pick up duties of their own. That is their analysis to run.

## Limits

This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves, MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere, each of which has its own implementing act and its own language rules. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

Web search is blocked in this session, so the German national-law citation below is from my own knowledge and you should verify the current MPDG text before acting on it. The MDR-level analysis is solid.

## Short answer

Your distributor is overstating it. "Everything has to be in German" is wrong as a blanket statement — but for the Declaration of Conformity specifically, they are probably right, and translating it is the low-cost move regardless.

## The legal hook

**MDR Article 19(1), final sentence** is the operative provision:

> The EU declaration of conformity shall be translated into an official Union language or languages **required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available on the market.**

So the MDR itself does not mandate translation. It delegates the decision to each Member State. The answer is therefore not "yes" or "no" at EU level — it's "whatever Germany has legislated."

## Germany specifically

Germany's implementing act is the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz). Its language provision requires German for the label and instructions for use, and my understanding is that Germany has exercised the Article 19(1) option to require the DoC in German as well. **Verify this against the current MPDG text (the Sprachenregelung section, § 8) and BfArM guidance** — I could not confirm the section number or current wording without web access, and this is exactly the kind of detail that gets amended.

Note that this is a separate question from **Article 10(14)** (documentation produced to a competent authority on request, in a language that authority determines). Germany is generally pragmatic about accepting English technical documentation under that route. Don't let anyone conflate the two — a distributor citing "the authorities accept English" is answering the wrong question.

## Where the distributor is wrong

Worth pushing back so this doesn't become a precedent for every document they ask for:

- **Label and IFU** — German, yes, non-negotiable (Art. 10(11) + Annex I 23.1(d) + MPDG).
- **Declaration of Conformity** — German, per the above.
- **Technical documentation, clinical evaluation, PMS plan, risk management file** — no. These are not "made available" to the German market. English is standard and accepted.
- **The DoC does not have to ship with the device.** Unlike some other CE regimes, MDR doesn't require the DoC to accompany each Class IIa unit to the end user. The distributor's actual obligation is **Article 14(2)(b)**: verify that a DoC *has been drawn up*. That's a verification duty, not a distribution duty. If they're asking for translated copies to hand to hospitals, that's a commercial ask dressed as a regulatory one.

## What I'd do

Issue a **bilingual DoC** — English and German in parallel columns or stacked on one page, single document, single revision number. Reasons:

1. It's one page. The translation cost is trivial next to the argument you're currently having.
2. It removes the question permanently for Germany and for German-language tender and hospital procurement, where a German DoC gets asked for whether or not law requires it.
3. One document means one version to keep current. Article 19(1) requires the DoC to be **continuously updated** — separate per-language files are how you end up with a stale German version contradicting a current English one during an audit.

State explicitly on the face of the document that the **English version is the authoritative text** in case of discrepancy. That protects you if a translator introduces an error in a scope statement or a standards list.

If you're selling into other markets too, apply the same Article 19(1) analysis per market rather than per distributor request — several Member States require their own language, and you'd rather find out once and batch the translations than one distributor complaint at a time.

One caveat on scope: I've treated this as a Class IIa device under a Notified Body certificate with Germany as an established market. If you're also relying on the DoC for a market where you use an authorised representative or a different conformity assessment route, the per-market language obligation still attaches independently.

## Short answer

Your distributor is overstating it. "Everything into German" is correct for **labelling and IFU**, but the Declaration of Conformity follows a different rule, and Germany is one of the Member States that does **not** require a German DoC.

## The legal chain

**Article 19(4) MDR** is the controlling provision:

> The EU declaration of conformity shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available.

So the MDR itself doesn't mandate any particular language — it delegates the choice to each Member State where you make the device available. The question is therefore not "what does the MDR say" but "what has Germany required."

**Germany's national implementation** is the MPDG (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz). Its language provision (§ 8, *Sprachenregelungen*) requires German for the Annex I Chapter III Section 23 information — label, IFU, implant card — but my understanding is that it permits the EU declaration of conformity in **German or English**. Germany is generally grouped with NL, IE, and the Nordics as English-accepting for the DoC, in contrast to FR, IT, ES, PL, where the national language is required.

⚠️ **Verify this before you rely on it.** I could not confirm the current wording of MPDG § 8 in this session. Pull the consolidated text from gesetze-im-internet.de and read the DoC sentence yourself — this is a one-paragraph check and it's the whole basis of the answer.

## What *does* have to be German

This is probably where your distributor's confusion comes from — several things genuinely must be German, so a blanket claim feels right to them:

| Item | German required for DE market? |
|---|---|
| Label (Annex I 23.2) | **Yes** |
| Instructions for use (Annex I 23.4) | **Yes** |
| Implant card + accompanying info (Art. 18) | **Yes** |
| Field safety notices (Art. 89) | **Yes** |
| **EU Declaration of Conformity** | **No — English accepted** (pending your § 8 check) |
| Technical documentation | Language agreed with your notified body; competent authority may demand German under Art. 10(14) |

Also worth correcting a common distributor assumption: the MDR does **not** require the DoC to ship with the device. Unlike the Machinery Directive, there's no accompanying-document obligation. Art. 10(8) requires you to keep it available to competent authorities for 10 years after the last device is placed on the market (15 for implantables). The distributor's own duty under Art. 14(2)(a) is only to verify that a DoC *has been drawn up* — not to hold it in German.

## Practical recommendation

Even though you're almost certainly not obliged to: **issue a single bilingual DE/EN DoC** rather than refusing, or rather than maintaining two separate files.

The reason is commercial, not regulatory. German hospital procurement, tender submissions, and Einkaufsgemeinschaften routinely ask for a German DoC, and arguing Art. 19(4) with a purchasing department is a poor use of your regulatory affairs time. The cost is one page of translation.

Do it as **one document with one revision number**, two columns or two stacked language blocks — not as two independent documents. Art. 19(1) requires the DoC to be kept continuously updated, and every separate language file is another artifact that can drift out of sync when you add a variant, change your notified body certificate number, or update the Basic UDI-DI. A single bilingual artifact under one change-control record avoids that failure mode entirely.

One thing to check while you're in there: if your device also falls under other Union legislation requiring a DoC (e.g. RED for a wireless component), Art. 19(3)–(4) requires a **single** combined declaration covering all applicable acts — and the language rule then has to satisfy every regime involved, which is not necessarily the same set.

**Bottom line:** you can decline on the legal merits, but supply a bilingual DoC anyway — confirm MPDG § 8's DoC sentence first so you're arguing from the actual text if the distributor pushes back.

Short answer: **the DoC is subject to a translation requirement under the MDR, but whether *Germany* triggers it is a national-law question — and for Germany the answer is most likely no.** Your distributor is right that the DoC is not exempt, and wrong that "everything" must be in German.

One caveat up front: I tried to pull the current text of the German MPDG to confirm the specific provision and web access is disabled in this session. The MDR side below I'm confident in; the German national provision is the part you should verify against the current statute (or have your German-market regulatory consultant confirm in writing).

## The MDR position

Article 19(1) MDR, final sentence:

> The EU declaration of conformity shall... be translated into an official Union language or languages **required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available on the market**.

So the MDR itself doesn't mandate German. It defers to each Member State. The default is that your English DoC is fine unless a Member State has affirmatively legislated a language requirement for the DoC.

## Germany specifically

Germany's language rules sit in the MPDG (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz), §8. The structure is:

- **Label and IFU** (Annex I Section 23 information) → German. This is the hard requirement, and it flows from Art. 10(11) MDR plus MPDG §8. There's a narrow carve-out permitting English IFU for devices used exclusively by professional users under defined conditions — check whether your Class IIa device qualifies, and don't assume it does.
- **EU Declaration of Conformity and technical documentation** → Germany accepts German **or English**. Germany is one of the more permissive Member States here; it does not impose a national-language DoC requirement on manufacturers placing devices on the market.

That second bullet is the one to verify against the current MPDG text. If it holds, your English-only DoC is legally sufficient for Germany.

## Where your distributor's confusion comes from

Distributors have their own verification duty under Art. 14(2) MDR. Before making a device available they must check that:

- (a) the device is CE marked **and an EU DoC has been drawn up**
- (b) the device is accompanied by the Art. 10(11) information — i.e. **label and IFU in the required language**
- (d) a UDI has been assigned

Note the asymmetry: the language requirement in (b) attaches to the labelling and IFU, not to the DoC in (a). For the DoC, the distributor only has to confirm it *exists*. Your distributor is reading the language condition in (b) across onto (a).

## What I'd actually do

Translate it anyway — but for commercial, not legal, reasons:

1. **It's a one-page document.** The cost of translating Annex IV content is trivial against the cost of this argument recurring with every distributor in every market.
2. **German tenders and hospital procurement routinely ask for a German DoC** regardless of what the law requires. Handing one over is faster than explaining Art. 19(1) to a procurement officer.
3. **Issue it as a single bilingual EN/DE document**, not two separate files. Two files means two documents to keep in sync every time you revise the DoC (new NB certificate, new product variant, Basic UDI-DI change), and a stale translated DoC in circulation is a genuine problem. One bilingual document with parallel columns has one version number and one signature.

If you'd rather not, you're on solid ground pushing back — but get the MPDG §8 confirmation in writing first so you have something to send the distributor.

## Two things worth checking while you're here

- **Your other markets.** Language requirements for the DoC genuinely do vary, and some Member States are stricter than Germany. Since Art. 19(1) points at each market's national law, "English is fine for Germany" tells you nothing about your other markets. Worth building a small matrix of DoC language requirements per market you sell into — this question will come back from every distributor otherwise.
- **Your German IFU and labelling.** This is the requirement with real enforcement exposure, and it's the one the distributor is actually obliged to verify under Art. 14(2)(b). If they're raising language issues, make sure that side is genuinely clean before the conversation turns to it.

This is regulatory information rather than legal advice — for the MPDG §8 confirmation specifically, get it from your German regulatory counsel or consultant, since that's the load-bearing point.

## Can the instructions for use be English-only? (IVD benchtop analyser, German hospital labs)

**German market:** confirmed — sold to hospital laboratories in Germany, so MPDG applies.
**Answer:** No, not as stated. English for the body of the IFU is available to you, but **safety-related information must still be provided in German** (or the user's language) — so "English only" fails § 8(2).

| Item | MDR/IVDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or** English — English alone is fine, no translation needed | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| Information for users (IFU, labelling) — default | not carried here | **German**, and it is a condition of supply: products may only be handed over to users if met | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, where use is exclusively professional | not carried here | English or another easily understood language permitted — but only in a *justified case* (*begründeter Fall*) | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information, even under that exception | not carried here | **German** or the user's language. The exception does not reach it. | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2, final clause `[verified]` |

### The three conditions are cumulative

§ 8(2) sentence 2 permits English only where **all three** hold:

1. it is a **justified case** — *begründeter Fall*;
2. the information is **exclusively** for professional users;
3. **safety-related information is still provided in German** or the user's language.

Your facts satisfy condition 2 cleanly — benchtop analyser, hospital labs, never patients or home users. But condition 2 is not self-executing: being professional-only is one of the three requirements, not the justification for the other two. And condition 3 is the one that breaks a pure English-only plan. The workable shape is a **bilingual package**: English IFU with the safety-related content in German — warnings, precautions, contraindications, residual-risk and handling instructions, and anything else your risk file treats as risk-control-by-information. Where the line falls between "safety-related" and the rest is a judgement call the statute does not itemise, and I won't state how BfArM or a German court would draw it.

### On the competitor

That a German competitor ships English-only is not a legal basis, and it does not tell you what their German-language content looks like or whether anyone has examined it. § 8(2) sentence 1 makes compliance a **condition of supply** — the exposure sits with you at handover, not with the precedent.

### Adjacent, since it is the same section family

If you ever take a field safety corrective action in Germany, the **Field Safety Notice must be written in German** (MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]`) — including for IVDR devices, the section names Art. 84(8) of 2017/746 expressly. No professional-user exception there. Worth knowing before you build a monolingual-English documentation pipeline you would have to break in an emergency.

**What would change this:** if the analyser were ever made available outside exclusively professional use, condition 2 fails and the full German requirement in sentence 1 applies to all user information. Conversely, nothing about hospital-lab sophistication removes condition 3 — the safety-content-in-German duty holds regardless of how fluent your users are.

(Standard caveat: this is regulatory orientation, not legal advice. Confirm with German regulatory counsel or your notified body before you freeze the documentation plan.)

## Where the requirement comes from

A benchtop analyser for hospital labs is an IVD, so **Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR)** applies — assuming it's placed on the market as an IVD and not as RUO/general lab equipment, which is a different regime entirely.

IVDR doesn't set the language itself. Annex I, Section 20 and Article 10 push the decision down: the information supplied with the device must be in a Union language **determined by the Member State in which the device is made available**. So the answer is entirely a question of German national law.

## What German law says

The relevant provision is **§ 11 MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz). The default rule is German. The exception — carried over in substance from the old § 11 MPG — permits the **instructions for use in English for devices intended exclusively for professional users**.

Two things I'd verify against the current statutory text rather than take from me:

- **The exact conditions attached to the exception.** The historical formulation conditioned it on the professional user's agreement, and there is a carve-out keeping **safety-relevant information and the label/packaging markings in German** even when the IFU may be English. Whether and how that applies to your product is the crux of the question, and it's worth reading the current wording plus any BfArM position rather than relying on a summary.
- **That "exclusively professional" holds across your entire distribution chain.** This is the condition that actually breaks in practice. If a distributor can resell to a physician's office lab, a POCT setting, a veterinary lab, or anywhere a non-professional operator touches it, the exception stops applying — and your controls, not your intent, are what an authority will look at.

## What English-only probably does *not* cover

Even if the IFU exception applies cleanly:

- **Label and packaging markings on the device itself** — plan for German unless you confirm otherwise.
- **Field safety notices and any vigilance communication to users** — these go out in German. Build the translation capability now; you don't want to be sourcing a translator during a recall.
- **Interactions with the competent authority** (the Land-level market surveillance body, not BfArM, for inspections) — they can request German-language material.
- **The EU Declaration of Conformity** — Article 17 requires translation into the language(s) the Member State requires; check Germany's position.
- **eIFU**, if you're going electronic under Regulation (EU) 2021/2226, is a separate permission and doesn't change the language analysis.

## Two things that will bite you outside the regulation

**The competitor is not evidence.** They may be reading the exception the same way you are, they may have a different intended-use statement, or they may simply not have been inspected yet. None of that transfers to you.

**Hospital procurement may require German regardless of what the law permits.** Under MPBetreibV the operator has duties around instructing users (Einweisung) and operating per the IFU. German hospital purchasing frequently makes German documentation a contractual requirement, and public-sector tenders often do so explicitly. You can be fully compliant and still lose deals.

1. Get a written opinion on § 11 MPDG applied to your specific intended use and distribution model — this is a cheap question for German counsel and it's the one that decides everything.
2. Tighten the intended-use statement and your distributor agreements so "exclusively professional users" is a controlled fact, not an assumption.
3. A benchtop analyser for hospital labs is an IVD under **Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR)**. IVDR Art. 10(10) does not itself set a language — it says the information in Annex I Section 20 must be in "an official Union language(s) **determined by the Member State** in which the device is made available." So the question is purely one of German national law.

Germany's implementing act is the **MPDG**, and its language provision (**§ 8 MPDG**) sets German as the default but contains an exception for devices supplied **exclusively to professional users**, under which the instructions for use may be in English. That exception carries conditions — as I recall it turns on the professional user's agreement and on safety not being compromised. Those conditions are the whole ballgame, and they're what you need counsel to read against your facts, not the headline permission.

## What stays in German regardless

Do not read the exception as "the whole product can be English":

- **Safety-relevant labelling and warnings** — the exception is narrower than the full Annex I Section 20 package; check how far it reaches beyond the IFU proper.
- **Field safety notices / FSCA communications** to German users and to BfArM — German, in practice always.
- **EU Declaration of Conformity** — IVDR Art. 17 requires translation into the language the Member State requires.
- **Technical documentation on request** — BfArM can demand German.
- **Summary of Safety and Performance** (if your analyser or its reagent system falls into class C/D and an SSP applies).

## The conditions are where this usually fails

"All our users are lab professionals" is doing more work in your sentence than it can bear. Your actual user population includes MTAs and lab technicians, night-shift staff, biomedical engineering and service technicians, and whoever does decontamination. "Professional" is not a synonym for "reads technical English under time pressure." Under IEC 62366 your usability engineering file and your risk management file need to positively justify that English does not raise use-error risk for *that* population — an English-only IFU is a design decision that has to survive your own risk analysis, not just a translation budget decision.

Also: once you ship into distribution you lose control of where units travel. Parallel movement into Austria brings a German requirement anyway; other Member States bring their own.

## The competitor argument

Discard it. Your competitor may be relying on the same exception and meeting its conditions, may be quietly non-compliant with nobody having complained yet, or may have a materially different intended-use statement. None of those is transferable to you, and none of it is a defence in a market surveillance action.

## Commercial reality, separate from legality

Your customers have their own obligations. Under **MPBetreibV** the hospital as operator must ensure users are instructed and have the IFU available, and under **ArbSchG / BetrSichV** the employer must give employees instructions in a language they understand. Several German hospital procurement departments turn this into a hard tender requirement for German documentation. So even where you may lawfully ship English, you can lose deals on it.

## What I'd recommend

1. Get German regulatory counsel to read § 8 MPDG against your intended-use statement and confirm exactly which documents the professional-user exception covers.
2. Document the decision in your technical file — risk management plus usability rationale, not just a commercial note.
3. Check your notified body's position early; some have views on this independent of the statute.
4. Consider German IFU with an English service manual as the split, or electronic IFU to cut the cost of doing German properly. The translation cost of an IFU is small next to one tender loss or one market surveillance finding.

## The MDR baseline

MDR doesn't itself name a language. It delegates:

- **Art. 10(11)**: the device must be accompanied by the Annex I §23 information "in an official Union language(s) **determined by the Member State in which the device is made available** to the user or patient."
- **Annex I §23.1(f)**: same rule restated for the content of the label and the IFU.
- **Annex I §23.4**: an IFU is mandatory here. The "no IFU needed if it can be used safely without one" exemption is only for Class I and IIa. **Class IIb ⇒ IFU always required.**

So your obligation is the union of what Spain and Portugal each demand. Two markets, two determinations.

## Spain

Baseline: **Spanish (castellano)**. The implementing act is **Real Decreto 192/2023, de 21 de marzo**, on medical devices (it replaced RD 1591/2009).

- Devices reaching a **lay user or patient**: labelling and IFU in Spanish, no discretion.
- Devices for **exclusively professional use**: Spanish law has traditionally allowed some relief here — under the predecessor RD 1591/2009 the IFU for professional-use devices could be in another EU official language while the safety-critical label information stayed in Spanish. RD 192/2023 carries a comparable split. **[verify the exact wording and scope of the professional-use carve-out in RD 192/2023 — this is the single most misapplied provision in Spain, and AEMPS can require Spanish regardless.]** My recommendation: ship Spanish anyway and don't build the launch around the carve-out.
- **Co-official languages** (Catalan, Basque, Galician): not required by the medical-device legislation. But if the device is retailed to consumers, Catalonia's consumer code (Llei 22/2010) creates a Catalan-labelling expectation for products distributed there. Low enforcement risk historically, non-zero for a lay-user product. Ignore it for a hospital-only device.

## Portugal

Baseline: **Portuguese**, and Portugal is the stricter of the two in practice — INFARMED has consistently expected Portuguese for information delivered with the device, including in hospital settings, and is less accommodating of English-only professional IFUs than AEMPS. The national MDR implementing decree-law (successor to DL 145/2009) keeps this. **[verify the current decree-law citation and its language article with INFARMED before quoting it.]**

Practical read: **plan on full Portuguese IFU and label.** Don't budget for an English-only professional exemption.

## What else is language-bound (easy to miss)

| Item | Rule | Applies to you? |
|---|---|---|
| Label | Same MS-determined language as IFU | Yes — ES + PT |
| **Declaration of Conformity** | Art. 19(1): translated into the language(s) required by each MS of availability | Check whether ES/PT require translation; many MS do. (This is the exact duty MPDG § 8 imposes in Germany — not your problem here) |
| **Implant card + patient info** | Art. 18: language determined by the MS | Only if your IIb is implantable — and the patient-facing text must be lay-comprehensible |
| **SSCP** | Art. 32 | Class III and implantables only — a non-implantable IIb has none |
| **FSN** | Art. 89: language accepted by each MS | Yes — pre-translate an FSN template into ES and PT now, not during an incident |

## Format and delivery

- **One multilingual IFU booklet covering ES + PT is fine.** Nothing requires country-specific print runs. Watch Annex I §23.1(d) legibility as you add columns.
- **Electronic IFU** under Reg. (EU) 2021/2226 is available for professional-use devices, but it doesn't relieve you of language: the eIFU must be available in the language of every MS where you make the device available, the website must serve those languages, and you must supply paper **free, within 7 days** of request. eIFU is essentially closed to lay-user devices.
- **EN ISO 15223-1 symbols** reduce translated text on the label but never substitute for the IFU language requirement.
- **Keep translation in-house.** Under Art. 16(3)–(4), a distributor or importer who translates your IFU takes on manufacturer-like obligations and must run a QMS covering it, and must notify you. Far cleaner to control translation under your own QMS, with the translated IFUs listed in the technical documentation your notified body reviews.

## Bottom line

Spanish and Portuguese IFU and labelling, full text, both markets. Treat the professional-use language carve-outs in each country as a fallback you've verified rather than a plan. No German obligations arise — but note that the moment a distributor makes the device available in Germany, MPDG § 8 pulls in German DoC and product information, so keep that condition explicit in your distribution agreements.

**European Portuguese is required.** National basis is the 2023 Decreto-Lei implementing the MDR (successor to DL 145/2009), administered by INFARMED.

- Portugal has historically been more permissive than Spain for devices intended **exclusively for professional use**, where English IFU could be accepted. Whether that survived into the current decree in the same form is the second point to verify. If you have a professional-only device and translation cost is material, it's worth checking; otherwise default to Portuguese.
- Use pt-PT, not pt-BR. Translations done for Brazil will not be accepted as-is.
- INFARMED device registration by the responsible entity expects the Portuguese labelling and IFU.

## Don't stop at the IFU — same language rule reaches further

| Item | Applies to you? | Language |
|---|---|---|
| Label and packaging text | Yes | ES + PT (EN ISO 15223-1 symbols cut translated text substantially) |
| EU Declaration of Conformity | Yes | Annex IV: translated into the language(s) required by each MS of availability — keep ES and PT versions |
| Implant card + patient information (Art. 18) | Only if your IIb is implantable | ES + PT |
| SSCP | Only if implantable or Class III — a non-implantable IIb needs none | Patient-facing part in ES + PT |
| Field Safety Notices | Yes, when one occurs | Must issue in ES and PT — have templates pre-translated, this is a vigilance duty and the clock is short |

Also note your **importers and distributors** in both countries are independently obliged to verify the device carries the required-language information (Art. 13(2)(b), 14(2)(b)). Non-localized stock will get rejected at the economic-operator level, not just by the competent authority.

**eIFU:** Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 permits electronic-only IFU for a closed list of categories (fixed installed devices, certain implantables/actives, software, accessories) and only for professional users, with a paper copy on request within 7 days and all required languages on the website. Assume paper unless you clearly fall inside a listed category.

## On Germany

Correct that MPDG § 8 (German-language DoC and product information) does not bite if you are not making the device available in Germany. Two things that could pull you in later, worth noting for your file rather than acting on now: a distributor onward-shipping stock into DE, and any future DE market entry — which would also bring DMIDS notification duties and German-language FSNs. An EU authorised representative located in Germany does not by itself trigger the language rules; *making available on the German market* does.

## Practical recommendation

Ship a single multilingual IFU covering ES + PT (permitted, and cheaper than two SKUs), with English retained as the master for your technical documentation and Notified Body. Bring translation under your ISO 13485 controls: qualified translators, back-translation or equivalent QC on safety-critical text, version linkage to the DoC and technical file, and — if the IFU carries any risk-control function — confirm whether your usability validation needs to cover the translated versions.

Short answer: Spanish and Portuguese. Nothing in German, and the MDR does not give you a "one language for the whole EU" option.

## The rule

MDR Article 10(11): the device must be accompanied by the Annex I §23 information (label, packaging, IFU) **"in an official Union language(s) determined by the Member State in which the device is made available to the user or patient."** Language is set country-by-country by national law, not by the Regulation. Because you're only making the device available in Spain and Portugal, only those two national rules bind you — Germany's does not, even if your notified body is German.

So: Castilian Spanish for Spain, European Portuguese for Portugal. A single bilingual ES/PT booklet is perfectly acceptable and is the normal Iberian approach.

## National specifics worth verifying against the actual text

- **Spain** — Real Decreto 192/2023 (which replaced RD 1591/2009). The baseline is that information reaching the final user or patient must be at least in Castilian Spanish. There is a carve-out in that decree relaxing this for devices intended exclusively for professional use; I'd read the language article of RD 192/2023 directly before relying on it, and in practice most manufacturers ship Spanish anyway because AEMPS and hospital tenders expect it.
- **Portugal** — Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2023. Same structure: Portuguese for information reaching the user or patient, with some flexibility historically recognised by INFARMED for strictly professional-use devices. Again, verify the language article rather than relying on the general practice.
- **Regional languages** — Catalan, Galician and Basque are not official Union languages for MDR purposes, so the MDR doesn't require them. But if your device is a lay-user/consumer device, Catalonia's Consumer Code (Llei 22/2010) can require permanent consumer information in Catalan. Irrelevant for a professional-use IIb; a real exposure if patients buy it.

## Other things the language rule reaches, not just the IFU

- **Label and packaging** — same rule, same two languages.
- **Declaration of conformity** — Article 19(1): must be translated into the language(s) required by each Member State where the device is made available. Have ES and PT versions ready.
- **Field safety notices** — must go out in the language of each affected market. Build the translation capability before you need it in a recall.
- **Implant card and patient information** — only if your IIb is implantable; then Article 18 information also follows the national language determination.
- **SSCP** — only required for Class III and implantables, so skip it unless yours is implantable.
- **Information to competent authorities** — Article 10(14): AEMPS and INFARMED can require submissions in their own official language. Technical documentation for your notified body is a separate negotiation (usually English).

## Two practical traps

**Don't let the distributor do the translating casually.** If your Iberian distributor translates the IFU or label, Article 16(2)(a) applies to them: they need a QMS covering translation, they must inform you before making the translated device available, and they must notify the competent authority. Cleaner to own the translations yourself and treat them as controlled documents under your QMS with back-translation or equivalent verification.

**Electronic IFU probably isn't available to you.** Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 limits eIFU to a narrow set — implantables and Class III for professionals, fixed installed devices, devices with a built-in display, and software. A typical non-implantable Class IIb doesn't qualify, so plan on paper. Even where eIFU is allowed, the language obligation is unchanged and you must supply paper free of charge on request within seven days.

**One forward-looking note:** goods move freely in the internal market. If a distributor later makes the device available in Germany — including through parallel distribution you didn't initiate — German IFU becomes a legal requirement and the device is non-compliant without it. Worth an explicit territorial restriction in your distribution agreements if you intend to hold the line at Iberia.

This is a regulatory summary, not legal advice; I'd have Spanish and Portuguese local counsel confirm the professional-use carve-outs in RD 192/2023 and DL 29/2023 before you rely on either to avoid a translation.

## The MDR framework

Language is not harmonised. MDR Art. 10(11) says the Annex I §23 information (label + IFU) must be supplied "in an official Union language(s) determined by the Member State in which the device is made available to the user or patient." Annex I §23.1(d) repeats this. So your obligation is the union of what Spain and Portugal each demand — nothing more.

**Germany is irrelevant to you.** No German, because you aren't making the device available there. The German requirement (MPDG §8 — German for the label and IFU) only attaches on placing/making available in Germany.

## Spain

Baseline: **Spanish (Castilian)**. That's the state-level requirement under the medical devices decree (RD 192/2023, which replaced RD 1591/2009).

⚠️ Verify: RD 1591/2009 carried a carve-out letting *professional-use-only* devices carry information in another language where the device doesn't reach the lay user. I believe RD 192/2023 keeps a version of this, but I can't confirm the exact article or its conditions without the text. If your Class IIb device is professional-use only and you were hoping to ship an English IFU into Spain, that hinges entirely on this clause — read it directly (BOE, RD 192/2023) rather than relying on my recollection.

Regional co-official languages (Catalan, Basque, Galician, Valencian) are **not** a medical-device requirement. Some autonomous communities have general consumer-labelling rules, but these are not normally applied to device IFU. Don't budget for them unless a regional tender or hospital contract asks.

## Portugal

Baseline: **Portuguese**. Set by the national implementing decree (DL 29/2023, replacing DL 145/2009).

⚠️ Verify: same pattern — Portuguese law has historically distinguished lay-user from professional-use devices, with INFARMED able to accept another language for the latter. Confirm the current article and whether it requires notification to INFARMED.

## Practical read

Assume **Spanish + Portuguese, both required, for label and IFU**, and treat any professional-use language relief as a bonus you only claim after reading the decree. The relief is narrow, conditional, and often evaporates at hospital procurement anyway — buyers ask for national language regardless of what the law permits.

## Things that travel with the IFU obligation

- **Declaration of Conformity** — Art. 19(1): must be translated into the language(s) required by each Member State where the device is made available. Spanish and Portuguese.
- **Field Safety Notices** — must go out in the language accepted by each Member State. Have translation capacity on standby; FSNs are time-pressured.
- **SSCP** — only if your Class IIb device is *implantable*. Then it's required (Art. 32) and must be in the languages the Member States determine. Non-implantable Class IIb: not applicable.
- **eIFU** — Reg. (EU) 2021/2226 is category-gated, not class-gated. Class IIb alone doesn't qualify you; you need to fall into one of the listed categories (fixed installed devices, implantables and their accessories for professional use, software, devices with a built-in display). Even then: paper IFU free on request, and the website must carry all required languages.
- **Symbols** — ISO 15223-1 symbols reduce translated text volume but don't discharge the language obligation for safety-critical instructions.

## One risk worth naming

You control where *you* make the device available; you don't control onward distribution within the single market. If a Spanish or Portuguese distributor resells into Germany, Art. 16(2)(a) puts the translation duty on that distributor — and Art. 16(3)–(4) then requires them to run a QMS covering it and notify you and the competent authority. In practice they'll come to you for the German IFU. Worth an explicit clause in your distribution agreements: territory restriction, or a requirement that they notify you before any onward cross-border supply.

This is general regulatory information, not legal advice — get the two decree articles confirmed by your regulatory counsel or Spanish/Portuguese local representative before you finalise the labelling spec.

## The governing rule

MDR (EU) 2017/745 **Article 10(11)**: the device must be accompanied by the Annex I §23 information "in an official Union language(s) **determined by the Member State in which the device is made available** to the user or patient."

So there is no EU-wide language. Your obligation is the union of Spain's and Portugal's national rules — Germany's (which requires German) is simply irrelevant to you. Class IIb matters here mainly because an IFU is always mandatory (the Annex I 23.1(d) exemption only reaches some Class I/IIa devices).

## Spain

- National implementing text: **Real Decreto 192/2023** (replaced RD 1591/2009).
- **Spanish (Castilian) is mandatory** for the information needed for safe use of the device, whenever the device reaches the end user or patient — this applies regardless of whether the user is a healthcare professional.
- There is limited flexibility for devices intended **exclusively for professional use**: remaining, non-safety-critical content may be accepted in another official EU language. Confirm the exact scope of that carve-out with AEMPS before relying on it — it is narrower than people assume.
- Co-official languages (Catalan/Valencian, Basque, Galician) are permitted additions, not substitutes. If the device reaches consumers, regional consumer-protection rules can push toward the co-official language in those communities.

## Portugal

- National implementing text: **Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2023** (8 May 2023).
- **Portuguese is the default requirement** for label and IFU.
- Portugal has historically been more permissive than Spain for **professional-use-only** devices, where English has been accepted in practice. This is exactly the point to verify with INFARMED in writing for your specific device — don't ship on the basis of past practice.

## The variable that actually decides your cost

Whether the device is **professional-use-only** or reaches lay users/patients:

- **Lay/patient-facing** → ES + PT translations, full stop. Annex I 23.1(d) additionally requires the IFU be readily understandable to the intended lay user, so plain-language adaptation, not just translation.
- **Professional-only** → ES still required for safe-use content; PT likely required but with a possible English route. Realistically: budget for both translations anyway.

## Don't forget these carry the same language obligation

- **Label and packaging** (Annex I §23.2), not just the IFU.
- **Declaration of Conformity** — into the languages required by ES and PT.
- **Implant card and patient information** (Art. 18) if your Class IIb device is implantable — language determined by each Member State.
- **SSCP** — required for implantable Class IIb; translated into the languages of the markets where the device is envisaged to be sold.
- **Field safety notices** (Art. 89) — ES and PT, at the point you ever need one.

## Two practical traps

1. **eIFU**: Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 only permits electronic-only IFU for specific categories and professional users, and you must still supply paper within 7 days on request — and in the required national language. It does not reduce your translation scope.
2. **Free movement**: CE marking means a distributor can lawfully move your device into other Member States. If that's foreseeable, your distribution agreements should control it, or you'll acquire a German-language obligation you didn't plan for.

Web access was denied in this session, so I couldn't verify against the consolidated statute — the MDR articles and procedural clocks below are solid, but **treat the MPDG paragraph numbers as pointers to verify** against the current text on gesetze-im-internet.de before you rely on them in a submission.

## Which regime applies

An unapproved Class III device studied to generate clinical evidence for conformity assessment falls under **Art. 62 MDR** (Reg. (EU) 2017/745) plus **Annex XV**. The MPDG doesn't replace this — it supplies the German procedure on top. Two consequences:

- This is a **"klinische Prüfung"**, not a "sonstige klinische Prüfung" (the MPDG §§ 47 ff. regime for non-CE-purpose studies). Don't let anyone route it there.
- **Art. 61(4) MDR** means a clinical investigation is *mandatory* for Class III and implantables unless you can invoke the narrow equivalence/legacy exemptions.

## Dual approval — both are required

| | Body | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Authorisation (*Genehmigung*) | **BfArM** — or **PEI** if the device integrally incorporates a blood-derived medicinal substance or human tissues/cells | MPDG (§§ 34–35 area) |
| Favourable opinion (*zustimmende Bewertung*) | A **registered ethics committee** (register per MPDG § 25 — only registered ECs can issue a valid opinion) | MPDG §§ 32–33 |

Key point for Class III: **Art. 70(7)(a) MDR** gives you **no tacit approval**. You need an explicit positive decision before enrolling the first subject. Starting without both the authorisation and the favourable opinion is a criminal offence under the MPDG penal provisions, not merely an administrative one.

Submission is a **single electronic application via DMIDS** (the German national portal), which routes to both BfArM and the EC running in parallel. The clinical-investigation module of EUDAMED was still not the mandatory route as of my information — confirm current status, since the Art. 78 coordinated assessment procedure becomes mandatory for multi-state investigations from **26 May 2027** and the portal picture is shifting.

## Deadlines (Art. 70 MDR)

| Step | Clock |
|---|---|
| Validation notice (in scope + complete) | **10 days** from receipt |
| Sponsor response if incomplete | **≤10 days** |
| Re-validation notice after response | **+5 days** |
| Authority silent on validation | Application **deemed validated** |
| Substantive decision | **45 days** from validation date |
| Extension for expert/clinical consultation | **+20 days** (65 total) |
| Request for information | Clock **suspended** from request until your response lands |

The EC's opinion is folded into that 45-day national clock — the EC must get its reasoned opinion to BfArM in time for the single decision. I'd verify the EC's internal sub-deadline in MPDG § 33 directly; that's the one figure I'm least confident reciting from memory.

**Realistic planning:** 3–4 months submission-to-approval with one RFI round, plus 2–4 months of preparation.

## EC submission dossier

Annex XV Chapter II is the backbone; the German additions are what trip up sponsors.

**Annex XV core:**
- Application form and the **single identification number**
- **Investigator's Brochure**
- **Clinical Investigation Plan** (Annex XV Ch. II §3) — endpoints, statistical rationale and sample size, risk-benefit analysis, stopping rules
- Declaration that the device conforms to the **Annex I GSPRs apart from the aspects under investigation**, and that every precaution has been taken for those aspects
- Technical documentation: risk management (ISO 14971), preclinical and bench data, biocompatibility (ISO 10993), sterilisation validation, software validation (IEC 62304), electrical safety (IEC 60601) and animal data as applicable, labelling and IFU
- Statement that the device was manufactured per applicable requirements
- **ISO 14155:2020** compliance statement

**German-specific / EC-focused:**
- **Probandenversicherung** — subject insurance certificate. This is a hard national requirement and a common rejection ground. The long-standing benchmark ECs apply is **€500,000 per subject**; confirm the figure the current MPDG text and your EC actually demand.
- **Subject information and informed consent forms in German**, plus GDPR Art. 13/14 data-protection information and BDSG-compliant consent
- Qualification evidence for the *Leiter der klinischen Prüfung* and each *Prüfer*: CVs, GCP/ISO 14155 training records, and **site suitability declarations** — the EC assesses persons and facilities, not just the protocol
- Sponsor–site contracts, investigator financial disclosures, funding sources, subject compensation
- Recruitment material, CRFs, subject diaries
- Disclosure of any prior EC opinion or refusal in another Member State
- **EU legal representative** if the sponsor is established outside the EU (Art. 62(2))
- Justification for any vulnerable population (incapacitated adults, minors, pregnant/breastfeeding subjects, detained persons) — the MPDG sets separate substantive conditions for each
- EC fee (varies by Land; typically low four figures to ~€6,000) and BfArM fee per the Kostenverordnung

If the investigation involves ionising radiation, you additionally need **StrlSchG** approval from the BfS — a separate track with its own timeline, so start it in parallel.

## Post-approval obligations with their own clocks

- **Substantial modifications (Art. 75):** notify; implementable at the earliest **38 days** after notification absent objection — and the EC must also concur
- **Safety reporting (Art. 80, per MDCG 2020-10/1):** SAEs with a causal relationship, device deficiencies that could have led to an SAE, and new findings — **≤2 calendar days** for events indicating imminent risk of death or serious injury requiring prompt remedial action, **≤7 calendar days** otherwise
- **End of investigation (Art. 77):** notify within **15 days**; **24 hours** for a temporary halt or early termination on safety grounds; clinical investigation report and lay summary within **1 year** of the end, or **3 months** after early termination

## What I'd do first

Nail down three things before drafting anything: whether BfArM or PEI is your competent authority, whether your sponsor needs an EU legal representative, and the insurance policy — those three drive the rest of the dossier and have the longest lead times.

This is regulatory orientation, not legal advice. Have German regulatory counsel or a consultant confirm the MPDG citations and current DMIDS/EUDAMED submission route; if you'd like, re-run this with web access enabled and I'll verify the paragraph numbers and the § 33 EC deadline directly against the statute.

I tried to pull the current statutory text (gesetze-im-internet.de for MPDG §§ 31–32) and to search, but **both WebFetch and WebSearch were denied in this session's permission mode**. So the below is from my own knowledge, with confidence flagged. The structural points I'm confident in; the exact day-counts and paragraph numbers you should confirm against the consolidated MPDG text before you rely on them — say the word and I'll re-run the lookups if you enable web access.

## 1. Which approvals you actually need

For a **non-CE-marked Class III device** under MDR Art. 62(1), Germany requires **two independent positive decisions**, and the study cannot start without both:

| | Body | Instrument |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory authorisation | **BfArM** (or **PEI** if the device integrates a medicinal substance derived from human blood/plasma, or otherwise falls in PEI's remit) | *Genehmigung* |
| Ethics review | A **registered** ethics committee (*registrierte Ethik-Kommission*) | *zustimmende Bewertung* |

Key point for Class III: MDR Art. 70(7)(a) gives you **no tacit approval**. For Class III and implantable/long-term invasive IIa–IIb devices you may start only once BfArM has *actively notified* you of authorisation. Silence is not consent — unlike the lower-risk categories in Art. 70(7)(b).

A negative ethics opinion independently blocks the study regardless of what BfArM decides.

## 2. Routing the submission

One application, submitted through **DMIDS** (Deutsches Medizinprodukteinformations- und Datenbanksystem), which distributes to both BfArM and the ethics committee — you do not file twice. The EUDAMED clinical investigation module is not yet mandatory, so DMIDS remains the route, but you still need the **EU single identification number (SIN)** from EUDAMED first.

The ethics committee is not freely chosen: it is the registered EC competent for the **coordinating investigator** (*Leiter der klinischen Prüfung*), named in the application. Only ECs registered with BfArM under MPDG may issue the opinion — verify your EC's registration status before you build the dossier around it.

## 3. Dossier contents

The master list is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II** — that governs, and MPDG adds national items on top. Core:

- Application form and SIN
- **Clinical Investigation Plan** per Annex XV Ch. II §3
- **Investigator's Brochure**
- Subject information sheet and informed consent form(s)
- Investigator CVs and qualifications; suitability of each site (*Eignung der Prüfstelle*)
- Declaration of conformity with Annex I GSPRs **except** the aspects under investigation, plus confirmation those aspects are covered by appropriate risk mitigation
- Risk-benefit analysis and risk management documentation
- Preclinical package: biocompatibility, sterilisation validation, electrical safety/EMC, software validation, animal data as applicable
- Manufacturing information, labelling, IFU
- Monitoring plan, CRFs, data management
- Statement on prior submissions/refusals in other Member States

**German add-ons:**
- **Subject insurance** (*Probandenversicherung*) — MPDG requires it, and the figure carried over from the old MPG regime is **at least €500,000 per subject**. *Confirm the current amount* — this is the number I'd most want re-verified.
- **Language**: subject-facing documents (information sheet, consent, insurance summary) must be **German**. Technical documentation is generally accepted in English by BfArM, but individual ECs vary — check your EC's own submission guidance.
- **GDPR/BDSG** data protection concept and consent to data processing.
- **Ionising radiation**: if the protocol applies radiation for research purposes, you need a *separate* approval or notification under **StrlSchG** (BfS involvement) — this runs on its own clock and is a common critical-path surprise.
- **Fees**: BfArM fee per the applicable cost ordinance, plus the EC's own fee schedule (set at Land level, typically low four figures).

**Vulnerable populations**: MDR Arts. 64–68 plus MPDG's stricter national provisions. Germany is notably more restrictive than the MDR baseline on non-beneficial research in adults lacking capacity — if your protocol touches this, treat it as a design constraint, not a paperwork item.

## 4. Deadlines

Validation (MDR Art. 70(5)) — these I'm confident in:
- **10 days** from receipt for the Member State to notify you whether the investigation is in scope and the application complete. Silence → deemed validated.
- If incomplete: you get **up to 10 days** to respond; the authority then has **5 further days** to notify. Missing your response window → the application **lapses** (you refile from scratch).
- The **validation date** starts the assessment clock.

Assessment:
- **45 days** from the validation date is the outer limit for the Class III authorisation decision, **extendable by 20 days** for expert consultation (→ **65 days**).
- MPDG sets an internal deadline for the EC to deliver its opinion so that it lands inside that window, and provides for a **single consolidated request for further information** (*Nachforderung*) which **suspends the clock** until you answer. I recall the EC's own deadline being somewhere in the ~26–30 day range from validation, but **I could not verify this and would not plan against my recollection** — pull MPDG § 32 directly.

Practical planning number: **~65–70 days from a clean validated submission to authorisation**, assuming no Nachforderung. One request for information realistically adds 4–8 weeks depending on your turnaround.

## 5. Clocks that start after approval

- **Substantial modifications** (Art. 75): notify, then a **38-day** standstill before implementing.
- **Safety reporting** (Art. 80): serious events posing a serious public-health threat — **2 days**; death or unanticipated serious deterioration — **7 days**; other reportable SAEs — **15 days**.
- **End of investigation**: notify within **15 days**; early termination within **15 days with justification**.
- **Clinical investigation report**: within **1 year** of end, or **3 months** of early termination.

## What I'd do next

Before drafting, pull three primary sources: the consolidated **MPDG** text (gesetze-im-internet.de), **BfArM's** clinical investigation procedural guidance, and **your specific EC's** submission checklist — ECs differ meaningfully on format, language and fee. The **Arbeitskreis Medizinische Ethik-Kommissionen** publishes harmonised templates worth starting from.

Two things genuinely worth verifying rather than trusting above: the €500,000 insurance minimum, and the EC's internal opinion deadline in MPDG § 32.

I tried to verify the section numbers and current deadlines against the primary sources, but web access is blocked in this session (permission denied in "don't ask" mode). So the below is from knowledge — the MDR-derived deadlines are solid, but **treat the MPDG paragraph numbers and the German-specific figures as pointers to check against the current consolidated text** before you rely on them. I've marked those.

## 1. The basic structure: two gates, one submission

For an unapproved Class III device being investigated to demonstrate conformity, you're in an **Article 62 MDR clinical investigation**. MPDG doesn't replace MDR here — MDR Arts. 62–82 and **Annex XV** carry the substance; MPDG (Abschnitt 4, roughly §§ 24–61) adds the German procedural layer.

You need **both**:

- **Zustimmende Bewertung** (favourable opinion) from a registered ethics committee — an EC registered with BfArM under MPDG. An unregistered university EC cannot give the statutory opinion.
- **Genehmigung** (authorisation) from BfArM as the *Bundesoberbehörde*. For Class III this is an **explicit** authorisation — Art. 70(7)(b) MDR. There is no tacit/silent approval, unlike Class I and non-invasive IIa/IIb.

Both go in as a **single submission through DMIDS** (Deutsches Medizinprodukteinformations- und Datenbanksystem), since the EUDAMED clinical investigation module isn't yet mandatory. BfArM validates and the two assessments then run **in parallel**, not sequentially — this is the single biggest planning difference from the old MPG regime. A negative EC opinion blocks the investigation regardless of what BfArM concludes.

> **Verify:** how the *competent* EC is determined — whether the sponsor selects freely from the registered list or it's tied to the *Leiter der klinischen Prüfung*'s Land. This has been amended and I don't want you planning around my recollection.

## 2. What goes in the submission

Core content is **Annex XV Chapter II MDR**:

1. **Application form** — DMIDS-generated, signed, with the single identification number.
2. **Investigator's Brochure** (Annex XV Ch. II § 2) — must be current and version-controlled.
3. **Clinical Investigation Plan** (Ch. II § 3) — structured per ISO 14155.
4. **Manufacturer's signed statement** that the device conforms to the General Safety and Performance Requirements (Annex I) *apart from* the aspects under investigation, and that every precaution has been taken regarding those aspects. For a Class III device this statement plus the supporting preclinical file is where assessors spend their time.
5. **Preclinical / technical and biological safety documentation** — biocompatibility (ISO 10993), electrical safety, software (IEC 62304), sterilisation, animal data, bench testing, risk management file (ISO 14971).
6. **Informed consent documents** — subject information sheet and consent form, **in German**.
7. **Proof of insurance / indemnification** for subjects.
8. **Data protection** — GDPR/BDSG-compliant concept, separate data-protection consent, and typically sign-off from the site's Datenschutzbeauftragter.
9. **Investigator CVs and qualification evidence**; suitability of the investigational sites and facilities.
10. **Financial arrangements** — subject compensation, investigator remuneration, funding sources, conflict-of-interest declarations.
11. **Recruitment material** — advertisements, screening scripts.
12. **Labelling** of the investigational device as "exclusively for clinical investigation" / *"nur für klinische Prüfungen"*.
13. **EU legal representative** if the sponsor is established outside the EU (Art. 62(2) MDR) — not optional.
14. Sponsor and investigator **QMS/monitoring plan**, safety reporting plan.

**German add-ons on top of Annex XV** — verify each against the current MPDG text:

- **Probandenversicherung.** A subject insurance policy is mandatory. The minimum sum carried over from MPG § 20 was **€500,000 per subject**; I believe MPDG retains this figure, but confirm it — it's the kind of number that gets adjusted.
- **Investigator qualification.** The *Leiter der klinischen Prüfung* / *Hauptprüfer* must be a suitably qualified physician; the historical German requirement was **at least two years' experience in clinical investigations of medical devices**. Confirm whether MPDG kept the two-year figure.
- **German-language requirements.** Subject-facing documents must be German. BfArM will generally accept English for the IB and technical documentation; ECs vary — many want the CIP synopsis in German. Ask your EC early, because translation is a real schedule item.
- **Professional-law (Berufsordnung)** consultation obligations for physician investigators via the Landesärztekammer.
- **Fees** — BfArM charges per its cost ordinance, and the EC charges separately under its own schedule. Budget both; I won't quote amounts I can't verify.

**Parallel procedure to watch:** if the protocol exposes subjects to **ionising radiation for research purposes** (research-only CT, X-ray, fluoroscopy beyond standard of care), you need a separate approval under the **Strahlenschutzgesetz** — a BfS *Genehmigung* under § 31 StrlSchG, or a notification under § 32 if it qualifies. This runs on its own clock and is frequently the critical path. It does not travel with the DMIDS submission.

## 3. Deadlines

**Pre-authorisation (MDR Art. 70):**

| Step | Clock |
|---|---|
| Validation — BfArM tells you if the application is in scope and complete | **10 days** from receipt. Silence → deemed valid. |
| If incomplete: your response window | **10 days** to comment/complete |
| BfArM re-validation after your response | **5 days**. Silence → deemed valid. |
| **Assessment** (Class III) — decision notified | **45 days** from the validation date |
| Extension for expert consultation | **+20 days** (so 65 days) |
| Requests for further information during assessment | Extends the period further; the clock effectively suspends |

The **validation date**, not the submission date, starts the 45 days. Build your Gantt chart from validation.

**During the investigation:**

| Event | Deadline |
|---|---|
| Substantial modification (Art. 75) | Notify; may implement **38 days** after notification absent refusal and absent negative EC opinion |
| SAE / device deficiency with imminent risk of death or serious injury | Immediately, **≤ 2 calendar days** from sponsor awareness |
| Other reportable SAEs and device deficiencies | **≤ 7 calendar days** *(per MDCG 2020-10; confirm — I've seen 3 and 7 cited)* |
| End of investigation in Germany (Art. 77(1)) | Notify within **15 days** |
| Temporary halt or early termination | **15 days** — but **24 hours** if halted on safety grounds |
| Clinical investigation report (Art. 77(5)) | **1 year** after end of investigation; **3 months** after early termination or halt |

Annual safety reporting to BfArM and the EC also applies.

## 4. Practical planning notes

- **A 45-day statutory clock is not a 45-day real timeline.** Between validation, a near-certain request for further information on a Class III preclinical package, and the 20-day expert extension, plan for roughly **3–4 months** from submission to authorisation, and more if the first submission bounces at validation.
- **Pre-submission meeting with BfArM** is worth requesting for an unapproved Class III device. It's the cheapest way to find out that your biocompatibility or animal data won't survive assessment.
- **The EC and BfArM assess different things.** BfArM: device safety, performance, preclinical evidence, benefit-risk. EC: subject protection, consent quality, investigator and site suitability, insurance, data protection, recruitment ethics. Don't assume a strong technical file carries the EC submission.
- **Class III + first-in-human** raises the bar on the CIP's risk mitigation, stopping rules, DSMB arrangements, and staged enrolment. Expect scrutiny there.

## What I'd confirm before acting

Because I couldn't reach the primary sources, please verify against the consolidated MPDG on `gesetze-im-internet.de` and BfArM's clinical investigation guidance:

1. The exact MPDG § numbers for the EC procedure and the authorisation procedure (I've deliberately not cited specific ones beyond the general range).
2. Whether MPDG sets a **shorter internal deadline for the EC's opinion** inside the 45-day window — I believe it does, so that BfArM can issue a consolidated decision, but I can't confirm the number.
3. The Probandenversicherung minimum sum and the investigator two-year experience requirement.
4. Whether the Medizinforschungsgesetz amendments touched the MPDG procedure — they were primarily AMG-focused, but there was some MPDG spillover.
5. Current BfArM and EC fee schedules.

If you can enable web access for this session, I'll pull the consolidated MPDG text and BfArM's guidance and give you a version with exact citations and a submission checklist you can hand to your regulatory team.

**German market:** confirmed in play (devices affected in Germany)

| Item | MDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Field Safety Notice language | Art. 89(8) governs the FSN; no language rule carried here | FSN **in deutscher Sprache** where the manufacturer takes an FSCA in Germany | MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]` |
| Who the German-language duty falls on | not carried here | Not limited to German-established manufacturers — § 73(1) is framed around the FSCA being taken *im Geltungsbereich dieses Gesetzes*. A US manufacturer with an Irish AR is still caught for the German devices. | MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]` |
| Documenting the FSCA + periodic effectiveness review | not carried here | Applies only to **manufacturers established in Germany** — on these facts, not you | MPDG § 73(2) s.1 `[verified]` |
| Notifying **completion** of the FSCA to the competent authority *and* the federal higher authority | not carried here | Falls on manufacturers, authorised representatives and importers **established in Germany**. You (US) and your AR (Ireland) are outside, so this does not land on you directly — but see below | MPDG § 73(2) s.2 `[verified]` |
| Importer completion notification | not carried here | A **German-established importer** must notify completion **because your AR sits outside Germany** (Ireland). - The German-language requirement is on the **FSN itself** (§ 73(1)), which is a separate hook from the general product-information rule in § 8(2). **What would change this:** if no affected devices were made available in Germany, § 73 would not apply at all and the English FSN would raise no German issue. Nothing else on these facts flips it — not your US establishment, not the Irish AR.

**On the other member states:** I can't help there. Germany's German-language FSN rule says nothing about what France, Italy, Spain or anyone else requires — each has its own implementing act with its own language provisions, and several do impose national-language FSNs. Assume English-only is a problem elsewhere too until checked country by country.

Yes — a few problems, and one of them (English-only into Germany) will very likely get your FSN rejected and re-issued.

## 1. Language: English-only doesn't work for Germany

Under MDR Article 89(8), the FSN must be in **the official Union language(s) determined by the Member State in which the FSCA is taken**. It's not the manufacturer's choice, and the fact that your AR is in an English-speaking country is irrelevant — the obligation attaches to each destination market.

Germany requires **German**. BfArM will expect a German-language FSN for distribution to German users, and will publish it. The same applies in most of the EU:

| Typically national language required | Often accept English (professional-use devices) |
|---|---|
| DE, AT, FR, IT, ES, PT, PL, CZ, SK, HU, RO, BG, HR, SI, GR, LT, LV, EE | NL, SE, DK, FI, (IE, MT — English is the national language) |

Two hard rules on top of that:
- **Lay users / home-use devices → always the national language**, even in the "English-tolerant" markets.
- **Belgium** needs NL/FR (and DE for the German-speaking community); **Luxembourg** FR/DE; **Finland** FI and SV for lay users.

Note the split: many competent authorities accept **English for the regulatory submission** (MIR/FSCA report to the CA), while still requiring the **local language for the FSN that reaches users**. Don't infer one from the other.

You remain responsible for translation accuracy — the risk and required-action sections especially. Use a translator who works in regulated medical content, and have your AR or local distributors review.

## 2. Sequencing: don't send it before the CAs have seen it

"We've drafted it and are sending it out" is the second issue. Standard practice under MDR and MDCG 2023-3 is to submit the draft FSN to the competent authorities of **every affected Member State** *before* distribution, and give them the opportunity to comment. Authorities routinely ask for changes to wording — particularly anything that reads as downplaying the risk. If you've already mailed it, you may have to issue a corrected version, which damages credibility with both regulators and customers.

Where several Member States are affected, ask whether a **coordinating competent authority** will be designated; that gives you one channel for comments instead of six divergent ones.

## 3. Other things worth checking before it goes out

- **Use the MDCG 2023-3 FSN template.** Authorities check for the mandatory elements: unique FSCA reference, device identification including Basic UDI-DI/UDI-DI and affected lots/serials, clear statement of the hazard and the risk, actions required of the user, the statement that the relevant competent authority has been informed, and a named contact. Missing fields are the most common reason for rework.
- **Acknowledgement mechanism.** Include a reply/acknowledgement form — you'll need it for the effectiveness check, which the authorities will ask about.
- **AR obligations (Art. 11).** Your Irish AR should be named, must hold a copy of the FSN and documentation, and must cooperate with CAs. Make sure they're actually looped into the submission, not just cc'd afterwards.
- **EUDAMED vigilance module.** Its mandatory-use status has been moving; confirm current requirements rather than assuming national portals still suffice — some of the affected CAs may now expect EUDAMED submission.
- **Non-EU markets in scope.** Switzerland (CH-REP, Swissmedic), UK/Northern Ireland (MHRA), Turkey — separate notifications with their own timelines and language rules.
- **US side.** As a US manufacturer, check whether this triggers 21 CFR 806 correction/removal reporting to FDA, and keep the messaging consistent across jurisdictions — inconsistent global FSNs get noticed.

## Suggested next step

Freeze distribution, build a matrix of affected Member State → required language → CA contact/portal → submission date, get the English master reviewed and approved, then translate and submit to the CAs in parallel. Distribute only after the comment window.

Happy to draft that matrix or check your FSN against the MDCG 2023-3 required elements if you paste the text. (This is regulatory orientation, not legal advice — confirm per-country language requirements with your AR or local regulatory counsel, since national practice does shift.)
